lines.trans: Folks, I gave up on being a candidate for city councilor.
Let's be honest, I don't have a proposal, I don't have anything.

Go on.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
I’m not going.

desistir.gloss: to give up; drop out; quit

meanings.en: to give up; drop out; quit
meanings.note: Takes de before what one quits: desistir de ser candidata (to drop out of being a candidate).

examples.trans: I gave up on being a candidate.
Calm down, don't quit now!

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.

examples.trans: It’s a marketing meeting.
I’m in finance.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
It’s a marketing meeting.

meanings.note: Takes the preposition a before the office sought: candidata a vereadora (candidate for city councilor).

examples.trans: I gave up on being a candidate.
She is a candidate for mayor.

meanings.note: Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.

examples.trans: She missed a meeting.
In an hour.

meanings.note: Member of a Brazilian municipal legislature (Câmara Municipal).

examples.text: Fui a vereadora mais votada da cidade.
examples.trans: I was the most-voted city councilor in the city.
She works as a city councilor.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Vamos combinar is a conversational opener meaning let's be honest / let's face it.

examples.text: Vamos combinar, eu não tenho proposta.
examples.trans: Let's be honest, I don't have a proposal.
We agreed to go out at eight.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.

examples.trans: No, I’m not going.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: A political proposal or business offer.

examples.trans: That is my proposal.
He accepted the proposal.

meanings.note: Used with nem or não for emphatic negation.

examples.text: Você nem comentou nada do implante?
examples.trans: You did not even mention anything about the implant?
I have nothing to say.

meanings.note: Often reinforced with é que in questions (como é que foi?).

examples.text: Como é que foi a cirurgia?
examples.trans: How did the surgery go?

examples.text: Como é que tá meu marido?
examples.trans: How is my husband doing?

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?
Are you in finance?

meanings.note: Doubled as já, já, it means 'very soon / any minute now'.

examples.trans: Your husband is already doing great.
I have already been in that situation.

meanings.note: Covers both using a tool/organ and wearing clothes.

examples.text: Essas camisas que a gente usa têm botão.
examples.trans: These shirts that we wear have a button.
Did my husband use all of this?

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: What is your job title?
Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Verba partidária refers to public campaign financing distributed by a political party.

examples.text: Você já usou a verba partidária.
examples.trans: You already used the party funds.
There was a lack of funds for the project.

meanings.note: Verba partidária refers to official political-party campaign funding.

examples.text: Você já usou a verba partidária.
examples.trans: You already used the party funds.
It was a party decision.

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.
What is this, man?

meanings.note: Takes a direct object for the thing paid for.

examples.trans: I will pay during the year.
Who is going to pay for the coffee?

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Pagar uma multa means to pay a financial penalty.

examples.text: Vai ter que pagar uma multa.
examples.trans: You are going to have to pay a fine.

examples.text: Ele levou uma multa no trânsito.
examples.trans: He got a traffic fine.

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.

examples.trans: See you later!
See you later. Thanks!

meanings.note: Ir até o final means to see something through to the very end.

examples.text: Agora você vai até o final.
examples.trans: Now you are going all the way to the end.
In the end everything worked out.

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Used for winning an election or prize as well as earning money.

examples.text: Se eu ganhar, não vou saber o que fazer.
examples.trans: If I win, I won't know what to do.

examples.text: Você não vai ganhar a eleição.
examples.trans: You are not going to win the election.

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Do you know the answer?

meanings.note: Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Used standalone in speech to mean of course / obviously.

examples.trans: I will need help, of course.
The explanation was very clear.

meanings.note: Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Is that what you want?

meanings.note: Quer garantia? asks whether someone wants a surefire guarantee.

examples.text: Quer garantia de que vai dar certo?
examples.trans: Do you want a guarantee that it will work?
This product has a warranty.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.

examples.trans: He is in the meeting.
She stays on her phone.

meanings.note: English loanword used across Brazil for video and audio interview shows.

examples.text: Vai num podcast e fala isso.
examples.trans: Go on a podcast and say that.
I listened to that podcast yesterday.

meanings.note: Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: Covers speaking, talking, and telling in everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.
examples.trans: Let me tell you something.
They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker; lá dentro reinforces inside there.

examples.trans: I'm going inside there.
Look in there.

meanings.note: Used for election matchups (contra Lula) and opposing a policy (ser contra o voto).

examples.trans: He is against that proposal.

examples.text: O jogo de hoje é contra eles.
examples.trans: Today's game is against them.

meanings.note: Used for individual ballots and election totals such as votos válidos (valid votes).

examples.trans: He got many votes.
We counted the valid votes.

meanings.note: O voto feminino means women's suffrage / women's right to vote.

examples.text: Ela falou sobre o voto feminino.
examples.trans: She spoke about the female vote.
The female audience loved it.

meanings.note: Conversational backchannel showing the listener is following or agreeing.

examples.trans: Uh-huh, I understand.
Mm-hmm, you can go on.

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: In the farewell até logo it anticipates meeting again. This is the time adverb, not a short form for a company logo.

examples.trans: See you later!
I’ll go to the meeting soon.
